questions.question: In GF(2), what operation corresponds to addition?
questions.explanation: Over GF(2), addition is mod 2, which matches XOR on bits.

questions.question: What does it mean for a binary code C ⊆ {0,1}^n to be linear?
options: If c1,c2 ∈ C then c1 ⊕ c2 ∈ C
If c ∈ C then reversing c is also in C
All codewords have the same Hamming weight
questions.explanation: Linearity means C is a subspace: closed under addition (XOR) and contains 0.

questions.question: A generator matrix G for a binary (n,k) linear code has which shape?
questions.explanation: G maps k-bit messages to n-bit codewords via c = m·G, so it is k×n.

questions.question: Given a parity-check matrix H, when is a word r a valid codeword?
options: When the Hamming weight of r is zero
questions.explanation: Codewords satisfy the parity constraints; the syndrome H·r^T must be the zero vector.

questions.question: If G is systematic in the form G = [I_k | P], what is a matching parity-check matrix form?
questions.explanation: In GF(2), H = [P^T | I] ensures G·H^T = 0, so every codeword has zero syndrome.

questions.question: In Hamming(7,4) syndrome decoding, why does a non-zero syndrome identify a single bit index to flip?
options: Each non-zero syndrome equals exactly one column of H
Because H is always the inverse of G
Because the syndrome is the message itself
questions.explanation: For Hamming(7,4), the columns of H are all distinct non-zero 3-bit vectors; they index bit positions.

questions.question: Attack scenario: what can happen if you apply single-error correction to a received word that actually has two bit flips?
options: You can miscorrect into the wrong valid codeword (wrong message)
You will always detect the two-bit error and refuse to decode
You will always recover the original message anyway
The syndrome must be 000 for any two-bit error
questions.explanation: Two-bit errors can produce the same syndrome as a one-bit error, so 'correcting' can flip a third bit and decode incorrectly.

questions.question: If a (7,4) Hamming code has minimum distance d_min = 3, what is the maximum number of errors it can guarantee to correct?
questions.explanation: A code corrects t errors when d_min ≥ 2t+1; with d_min=3, t=1.
